entries.text:
You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call and say the rest in Draconic, just above the water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

Silence. The sluice-water ticks over the stones. Then, from the dark inside, a voice you have not heard in fourteen years, older and rougher than you imagined, and wary as a cornered goat.

"Say how many goats come home."

You know it at once, the last line of the song, the one Dargan always changed for the little ones. "Seven go out," you say, and your voice cracks on it. "Seven come home. Even the lost one."

A figure steps out of the dark. She is small, hooded, and thin as a rail, with a dragonborn's red scales gone dull with soot and a left hand that is scarred across the knuckles. She stops an arm's length away and pushes the hood back. The face is Dargan's jaw and your mother's eyes, and she looks at you for a long moment as if you might be another trick of the dark.

"You're loud," says Tessa. "I heard you from the third gate." Then her face breaks, and she hits you in the chest with her good fist, once, hard, and after that she is holding on to your shirt with both hands and not saying anything at all.

When she can speak she does it fast and low, glancing at the arch. She has hidden in the rocks since the raid. Gorrak's patrols never caught her, and she knows now it was not luck. Last winter she took work as a mender at Greyshaft to get into the ledger-house, because she heard the Foreman keeps a book. "It's not tin," she says. "It's names. Children, from the steadings. Where they were taken, what they fetched, and the buyer, far south. I've copied three seasons of it." She taps her chest, where something is sewn inside her tunic. "The Foreman counts again on midwinter's eve. Four days. Whatever he has in his cells goes south that night, and the ledger goes with it. Once it's gone, nobody ever finds them."

She looks up at you, fierce and frightened. "Gorrak was never the worst of it, Kor. He's the Foreman's hand. I need the hand to turn."

It is near eleven at night. What does Korvash do?

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. Low and steady you hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say in Draconic, just above the water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long breath there is only the trickle. Then a pebble clicks, and a small figure steps out of the black of the tunnel with her hood up and a short knife held low and ready. She stops two paces away and does not lower it.

"Say the seventh goat," she whispers.

"It comes home," you say. "It always comes home."

The knife drops. She pushes back the hood.

She is nineteen now, wiry and small, with Dargan's jaw and your mother's eyes. Her scales are a duller red than yours, scuffed with soot, and there is a notched crescent stitched in thread on her cuff. She stares at you as though you might dissolve, and you see her chin tremble before she gets it under control, in a way that is very much a Dargan thing to do.

"You're so *loud*," she says, a shaky half-laugh, and then she is against your chest with her fists in your shirt, and neither of you speaks for a while.

When she pulls back she wipes her face hard and goes quickly to business, as if afraid of how long she can hold herself together. "I haven't got long. The Foreman keeps a second ledger, Kor, apart from the one you've seen. Every child he's taken, with their steading and where they were sent. I hid at the Weeping Ledge the night of the raid, and the hermit goat-folk raised me after. I came here at the autumn tally on purpose, as a mender, to find that book and get it out. Gorrak saw me that night and let me live, and I don't know why, and I don't trust it." She grips your wrist. "It's in the ledger-house, behind six sworn guards. I can't get it alone. And in four nights, at midwinter's eve, the Foreman reads the tally aloud, and your name goes into it for good."

The water runs past your boots. It is nearly half past ten, and your sister, alive, is holding your wrist in a culvert at the foot of an enemy wall. Four nights remain.

What does Korvash say and do?

input.add_to_description: Day 16 ~10:30 PM at the culvert: Tessa came out and met Korvash. (See narrated scene.) She is alive, about 20, small and wiry, hooded, with a notched ear-cuff of horn and a scar across her left palm. She has served as the Foreman's mender since autumn, placed there deliberately: she is hunting the Foreman's ledger, which lists every child taken from the clan steadings, including the names of those still alive in the mines. She knows Gorrak spared her and does not trust him. She asks Korvash to keep playing the bought man and to be at the ledger-house stair at dusk on Day 19.

entries.text:
You pull your boots on and wade out onto the flat stones, stopping at the mouth of the arch with your hands open and the handaxe still in your belt. The water is loud in the dark. Low and steady, you hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, and then say in Draconic, just above the trickle: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is nothing. Then a pebble drops somewhere inside, and a small figure steps out of the black, hood up, one hand on the wet wall. She stops three paces off. Starlight finds the edge of a jaw, a scarred palm, a horn ear-cuff with a notch bitten from its curve.

She pushes the hood back. She is twenty, small and wiry, with your father's jaw and a face that has forgotten how to be careless. For a heartbeat neither of you moves. Then she crosses the three paces and hits you in the chest with both fists, once, hard, and holds on.

You do not remember what you say. You remember that she shakes, and that you are loud even now, a wrecked whisper, repeating her name.

When she can speak she keeps it short, because the wall is close. She has lived. The night of the raid she ran up the high ledges and hid in the Weeping Ledge until the smoke cleared, and after that she was a goat among the rocks for years, with the cairn her one fixed point. In the autumn she came down and let the Foreman's recruiters take her, because the Foreman keeps a ledger of every child taken from the steadings, living and dead, and she wants it. "He writes down who is still in the galleries," she says. "Dozens. Names, steadings, shifts. Some from our own fold, Kor, children who were babies when we ran." She wipes her face. "Gorrak spared me once. I don't know why, and I don't trust it."

She presses a key-shaped sliver of horn into your hand, notched like her mark. "The ledger-house stair, dusk on the nineteenth. The six on the stair change at the bell, and there is one breath where the stair is empty. Be there, loud, with your axe, as a bought man looking for his bed. I'll do the rest." She grips your wrist. "Keep the face. Don't look at me in the yard."

She melts back into the culvert. You stand a long while in the cold water with a horn key in your fist, then walk back through the dark to your bunk, where Pip is snoring under his cap and the blanket has not been disturbed.

It is just after eleven at night on the sixteenth. You have the key, three days, and a plan with your sister's hand on it. What does Korvash do?

She wants Korvash to help get the ledger out of the ledger-house before midwinter's eve (4 days), when the Foreman ships the season's 'hands' to a buyer; the ledger names every taken child and where sent, and would let Harrowmere's villages reclaim them. Quest becomes: free Tessa and take the ledger.

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. Low, under the trickle of the water, you hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call and say it in Draconic: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is only water. Then a shape detaches from the dark of the tunnel, small and hooded, one hand on the wall and the other holding something against her chest. It is a bundle of cloth. She stops three paces off and pushes the hood back.

She has Dargan's jaw and Veshra's narrow eyes, and a thin white scar through one eyebrow that you do not know. She is not the child you lost. She is a young woman with ink stains to the wrists and needle-pricked fingers, and she looks at you the way you must have looked at the goat on the cairn.

"You got big," she says, and her voice cracks on it. "You were loud at the ford. I heard. Everyone in the ledger-house heard." She laughs, one wet breath, and then she is against your chest, and the bundle is crushed between you, and neither of you says anything in any language for some while.

When she can speak again, it comes fast and low. She went over the high ledge the night of the raid, small enough that Gorrak's man saw her and looked away. She lived in the rocks above the Throat for years on goats and trade, leaving cheese at the Seven Crooks. A season ago she heard the Tallies' tallies were kept at Greyshaft, so she took work as a mender of ledger-bindings, hooded and nameless, to learn what they hold. She unwraps the bundle: a thick, stitched ledger-page, hand-copied in her careful script.

"Every child the Tallies have taken, Kor, with the steading, the date, and where each was sent. Dozens of villages. Some of them are still alive." Her eyes are fierce. "The Foreman ships the season's hands to a buyer on midwinter's eve, four days from now. The true ledger is in the ledger-house, under six guards, and after the shipment it goes into the smelter fire. If we take it, Harrowmere and every village on this mountain can come for their own."

She looks at the axe you did not bring, at the sash you are not wearing, and finally at your face. "You swore a year and a day to him. I know. I'm not asking you to break it. I'm asking you what you'll do when it is your oath against all of them."

It is close to eleven at night on day sixteen. Tessa waits. What does Korvash say?

sheet.opening: Korvash Emberhide, a hulking red-scaled dragonborn barbarian (Chaotic Good, loud, proud, quick to anger; ideal Charity; bond: he keeps his word no matter what; flaw: inflexible), arrives at dusk in a lowland market town near the foot of the mountains, driving off a pack of bullies shaking down a family of herders, as he has done for years. His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. entries.text:
You pull your boots on, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open and the handaxe still in your belt. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call and say her name into the dark, low, in Draconic, just above the trickle of the water.

For a long moment there is only the water. Then a voice answers from deep in the culvert, thin and even, in the same tongue. "Say the number of the lost goat."

You don't need to think. "Seven. And he comes home on the third night, by the water, with burrs in his coat."

A small figure steps out of the black, hooded, one hand holding a cloth-wrapped bundle and the other held a little away from the knife at her hip. She stops an arm's length from you. She is smaller than you ever pictured, narrow-shouldered and red-scaled, with a burn-pink scar along one jaw and your father's amber eyes. She pushes back the hood.

"You're so loud," Tessa says, and her voice cracks down the middle. "I heard you coming from the cairn. I heard you calling for two nights on the east path and I lay in the rock and didn't answer, and it was the hardest thing I've ever done." She laughs once, wet and fierce, and then she has crossed the distance and her face is pressed hard against your chest, her fist knotted in the sash on your belt where the haft's twin would be, and she is shaking.

You hold your sister. Fourteen years go through you and out.

When she steps back she wipes her face and is all business again, a person who has had a long time to learn how. She tells it fast and low. She was eight. She hid in the Weeping Ledge while the raid burned the village and crept out into silence afterward, and she lived on rock-goats and seep-water until the old shepherds of the high steadings took her in and gave her a name that wasn't hers. Gorrak Vael saw her once, at the Throat, and let her go. Two seasons ago she learned that the Foreman keeps a ledger of every hand taken from every clan village, names and steadings and dates. Hers is in it. So is Dargan's, so are all the lost ones, and so, she believes, is the answer to who sold the Tallies the way up the pass. "I came in with the autumn tally to get that book," she says. "I'm a mender. Nobody looks at a mender."

She looks past you up the slope at the dark shape of the third gate. "It sleeps in the ledger-house, in an iron chest, under six Tally-sworn on the stair and the Foreman's own bed. I need an axe, Kor. I need yours. And I need you to keep playing the bought man for four more days."

She holds out the cloth bundle. Inside is a folded sketch on scraped hide, a plan of the ledger-house stairs.

It's nearly eleven. The second night bell is long past, and Pip will wake at dawn. What does Korvash say to his sister?

She survived the raid hiding in the Weeping Ledge, was fed for years by a hermit shepherd, and after he died took work with the autumn tally to get inside Greyshaft. entries.text:
You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open and the handaxe still in your belt. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say it in Draconic, just above the trickle of the water: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long moment there is only the water. Then a shape detaches from the dark of the tunnel, small and quick, and stops two paces off with a wet cloth bundle clutched to her chest. The hood comes down. Red scales, dull in the dark and worn at the edges. A notch in one horn-frill. A jaw you have seen every morning in your aunt's face and your father's. She is grown, harder than you remember, and her eyes are wet.

"You're loud even when you whisper," says Tessa.

You don't remember crossing the rocks. She is solid and cold and smells of lamp-oil and wet wool, and she is crying into your chest and hitting your shoulder with the flat of her fist, both at once. "You took fourteen years," she says into your shirt. "I left you a *goat*, Kor."

When you can both speak, she tells it fast and low, glancing up at the wall. She hid in the Weeping Ledge the night of the raid and lived there for years on a hermit shepherd's charity, an old man who never gave his name and who died two winters ago. After that she took work with the autumn tally as a mender, to get inside Greyshaft, because she had learned what the Foreman's ledger holds. "Every child he's ever taken, written down by name and steading. Ours too. Eleven from our village, Kor. Alive, most of them, in the lower galleries. Some are grown now." Her fingers dig into your arm. "On midwinter's eve he does the annual count. Whoever is on the list goes out on the convoy, sold on south. Four days. After that they are gone, and I have only the ledger to follow."

Above you, a bell tolls the third hour of the night. The wall guards' laughter drifts down, thin and drunk. Tessa wipes her face and looks at you hard, a stranger and your sister.

"Gorrak knows I live," she says. "I think he's been protecting me. I don't know why, and I don't trust it. Tell me what you swore, and what you want to do."

It is nearly eleven at night. Pip sleeps in the barracks; the Foreman's ledger sleeps in the third gate. What does Korvash say and do?

You pull your boots on, wade onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, then say it in Draconic, barely above the trickle: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

Silence, then a small sound, the scrape of a nail on stone. A figure unfolds from the dark of the culvert, hooded and slight, and stops five paces off with a hand on a mending-knife. She does not come closer.

"Say something only Kor would know," she says. Her voice is rough from disuse, but it is a voice you know.

You answer without thinking. "You cut your crescent into my boots the winter you were six, and I wore them anyway, and Father pretended not to see."

The knife drops. She pushes back her hood. Red scales dulled with soot, a scar through one brow, Dargan's jaw, and eyes as wet and furious as yours. She crosses the five paces in a breath and hits you in the chest with both fists, then hangs onto your shirt and does not let go. Neither of you says anything for a long while. Water runs. Up on the wall, someone laughs at a joke.

She grew up in the rocks and the Weeping Ledge, trading cheese. She came to Greyshaft in autumn, hooded, as a mender, for one reason. "The Foreman keeps a ledger of every hand he's taken. I mended the bindings and I read it, Kor. Our people from the raid, the ones nobody saw fall. They didn't die. They were sent here. They're listed as living, in the deep galleries below the third gate." Her grip tightens. "I haven't found the way down. Six Tally-sworn on the stair, and the Foreman himself sleeps up there."

She wipes her face with a sooty wrist. "Wait for midwinter's eve. The Foreman holds a tally-feast in the Counting House and the third-gate guard goes down for it. That's our night. Until then, don't know me. Don't look up. He's cleverer than he sounds."

entries.text:
You pull your boots on, wade out onto the flat rocks, and stop at the mouth of the arch with your hands open. You hum the first three notes of Dargan's evening call, low, and speak into the dark in Draconic: "Tess. It's Kor. Nobody followed me. Come out where I can see you."

For a long breath there is only water. Then a pebble clicks inside the tunnel, and a small figure steps into the thin light from the smelter glow. Hooded, cloaked in patched grey, a head shorter than you. She pushes the hood back with a scaled hand. Her scales are the deep red of the clan, her left horn is chipped, and her face is your father's, narrower and harder, with a scar through one brow. She has your mother's eyes. You know them the way you know your own name.

"You're loud even when you whisper," says Tessa. Her voice breaks on the last word.

Then she hits you in the chest with both fists, once, hard, and holds on. You hold her. Neither of you says anything for a time, and the water goes on running over the stones.

When she can speak she tells it fast and low, glancing at the arch's mouth. She was seven the night of the raid. She hid in a crack above the Throat and watched Dargan hold the pass until he fell. An old hermit goatherd found her at dawn and raised her in the rocks, and he died two winters ago. She left the goat at the cairn each year. She came to Greyshaft last autumn on purpose, on the tally cart, because the hermit had told her where taken children are sent. The Foreman needed a mender who could read, and she has been mending his ledger-bindings ever since, and reading the pages as she goes.

"It's all written down," she whispers. "Every child, every steading, every shipment: the deep galleries, and a buyer in the lowlands. Your thirty-one were meant for the next cart. Gorrak's oath to you cost the Foreman a season's quota, and he knows it." Her jaw sets. "On midwinter's eve the full tally is counted, and the ledger is carried down to the Counting House. I have the key to the ledger-house stair. Wait for me until then. Don't do anything loud."

She almost smiles at that. "I know. But try."

She has to be back before the third bell, or the guards will count her missing. It is nearly eleven at night, there are four days to midwinter's eve, and the one person you ever swore to find is holding your sleeve.

When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. I set the boy down, tell him "Run to Tessa, lad, and don't stop," and climb onto the rubble heap with the shield up and the sword out, so the scouts have to look at me and not the column. Then I bellow up the gully in Goblin and Common alike, as loud as my cracked voice will go: "Two grey cloaks on a ridge, and a whole camp's worth of me already past you! Come down and learn what a Tally's axe is worth, or go and tell your Foreman Dargan's son walked ninety-four children out of his mine!"

"Ninna, Tessa, keep them moving!"

You set the boy down and he bolts. You climb the rubble with the shield up and the sword out, and you roar. It cracks and rasps, but it carries up the walls of the gully in two tongues, and it rolls back down off the slate like a landslide: *a whole camp's worth of me already past you, come down and learn what a Tally's axe is worth, or tell your Foreman that Dargan's son walked ninety-four children out of his mine.*

The scouts do not come down. They were told to watch and count, and the thing on the rubble is not what they were told to count. The one with the sword looks at the bow-woman. Some silent agreement passes between them. He turns and goes back along the ridge at a run, toward Greyshaft and the bell, carrying your name with him. The bow-woman stays on the rim, and she does not loose. She keeps pace along the edge of the gully, always a long bowshot back, with the arrow still nocked and her eyes on the column.

Behind you the children are filing down the track with Ninna's whisper running along them. Tessa glances back once, hard, and you see her take in the name that has just gone up the hill.

It is nearly seven in the morning. The Foreman now knows exactly who you are, and he will know within the hour how many walked out. The track drops toward a stream and the high road beyond. The shadow on the ridge is waiting for the column to come out into the open. You are at 2 hit points.

What does Korvash do?

You climb onto the rubble with the shield up and bellow your challenge up the gully in Goblin and Common both. It cracks in the middle. The two grey cloaks do not move, because they can see one dragonborn with a bloody bandage and a boy's weight still in his arms, not a camp's worth of anyone. The archer's first two arrows go wide of the shield. The swordsman is down the slope before the echo dies, and his blade finds the gap under your arm. Your legs fold, and the second cut comes down on you already falling.

You hear one voice from a long way off. "Alive! The Foreman wants him alive!" Hands turn you over and press a wad of cloth against your side. Then there is only dark.

You wake with your cheek on cold slate, wrists bound behind you and the sun well up. It is nearly nine in the morning, and you have 1 hit point. Your sword, shield and keys are gone. The two scouts sit a few paces off on the lip of the gully, sharing a waterskin. Beside them a little knot of children sits roped together at the ankle, nine or ten, the smallest of them sniffling. Ninna is not among them. Nor is Tessa.

The archer sees your eyes open and grunts. "Your lot went to ground in the rocks like rabbits. Drilled them well, didn't you? We've got the slow ones. The rest will keep for the hobgoblins." He jerks his chin toward the black bowl of Greyshaft. A dozen torches are strung out along the track below, coming up in a long line, and a heavy tin-banded figure walks at the head of it with a measuring stride.

It is the Foreman, soft-voiced and in no hurry. The scout stands. "Morning, Emberhide. He'd like a word."

You set the boy down and send him running with a shove, then climb the rubble heap with the shield up and your cracked voice thrown up the gully in Goblin, then Common. It rattles off the slate like a falling cart.

It works, or enough of it does. The archer's string creaks and stays drawn. The swordsman looks at the length of the column, at the man on the rubble bellowing as though a hundred more stood behind him, and weighs it. They have seen the road, and they have seen you. They do not know you are held together by bandages and spite.

"Dargan's son," the swordsman says, quietly, in Common, as if tasting it. Then he is gone from the ridge like a man dropping into water, running back toward Greyshaft. The archer stays a long moment with the arrow on the string, her eyes on your face. She lowers the bow, steps back out of sight, and does not leave. She is still up there, keeping pace along the ridge.

You get the column moving. Tessa leads, Ninna counts, and your legs carry you at the rear. The gully opens onto a stream and a stony slope, and by seven you are well clear of the bowl. The alarm bell behind you has thinned to a faint tolling.

But the Foreman has your father's name now, and it is on its way to him. The ledger is still in its chest above you, and the day has barely begun. Tessa drops back beside you, looking at your pale face. "Kor," she says. "You can't keep walking on that. What do we do?"

features: Draconic Ancestry: You have draconic ancestry. Choose one type of dragon from the Draconic Ancestry table. Your breath weapon and damage resistance are determined by the dragon type, as shown in the table.

Breath Weapon: You can use your action to exhale destructive energy. Your draconic ancestry determines the size, shape, and damage type of the exhalation. When you use your breath weapon, each creature in the area of the exhalation must make a saving throw, the type of which is determined by your draconic ancestry. The DC for this saving throw equals 8 + your Constitution modifier + your proficiency bonus. A creature takes 2d6 damage on a failed save, and half as much damage on a successful one. The damage increases to 3d6 at 6th level, 4d6 at 11th level, and 5d6 at 16th level. After you use your breath weapon, you cannot use it again until you complete a short or long rest.
Damage Resistance: You have resistance to the damage type associated with your draconic ancestry.
Draconic Ancestry (Red): breath weapon 15 ft cone, DEX save DC 12, 2d6 Fire damage (half on a success); resistance to that damage type

Rage: In battle, you fight with primal ferocity. On your turn, you can enter a rage as a bonus action. While raging, you gain the following benefits if you aren't wearing heavy armor: - You have advantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. - When you make a melee weapon attack using Strength, you gain a bonus to the damage roll that increases as you gain levels as a barbarian, as shown in the Rage Damage column of the Barbarian table. - You have resistance to bludgeoning, piercing, and slashing damage. If you are able to cast spells, you can't cast them or concentrate on them while raging. Your rage lasts for 1 minute. It ends early if you are knocked unconscious or if your turn ends and you haven't attacked a hostile creature since your last turn or taken damage since then. You can also end your rage on your turn as a bonus action. Once you have raged the number of times shown for your barbarian level in the Rages column of the Barbarian table, you must finish a long rest before you can rage again.
Unarmored Defense: While you are not wearing any armor, your Armor Class equals 10 + your Dexterity modifier + your Constitution modifier. You can use a shield and still gain this benefit.

Shelter of the Faithful (Acolyte): As an acolyte, you command the respect of those who share your faith, and you can perform the religious ceremonies of your deity. You and your adventuring companions can expect to receive free healing and care at a temple, shrine, or other established presence of your faith, though you must provide any material components needed for spells. Those who share your religion will support you (but only you) at a modest lifestyle. You might also have ties to a specific temple dedicated to your chosen deity or pantheon, and you have a residence there. This could be the temple where you used to serve, if you remain on good terms with it, or a temple where you have found a new home. While near your temple, you can call upon the priests for assistance, provided the assistance you ask for is not hazardous and you remain in good standing with your temple.
